transcription.tex: \text{A circle has area \(A=\pi r^2\), so \(dA/dr=2\pi r\), its circumference.}
\text{Increase the radius by a small amount h.}
\text{The thin ring is approximately a strip of length 2πr and width h.}
\text{Divide by h and let h approach zero.}
\text{Adding these thin rings is integration: it recovers the area from its rate of change.}

transcription.tex: [STEP I 2014 Q3] The numbers \(a\) and \(b\), where \(b>a\ge 0\), are such that  \(\int_{a}^{b} {x}^{2} dx={\left(\int_{a}^{b} x dx\right)}^{2}\)\par In the case \(a=0\) and \(b>0\), find the value of \(b\).

In the case \(a=1\), show that \(b\) satisfies
\(3{b}^{3}-{b}^{2}-7b-7=0\)
Show further, with the help of a sketch, that there is only one (real) value of \(b\) that satisfies the equation and that it lies between 2 and 3.

\text{\[\frac{b^3-1}3=\frac{(b^2-1)^2}4\]Divide by b − 1, since b > 1:\[3b^3-b^2-7b-7=0\]For h(b) equal to this cubic, h(2) = −1 and h(3) = 44. Its turning points at −7/9 and 1 both have negative values, so it has exactly one real root, between 2 and 3.}
Show that \(3{p}^{2}+{q}^{2}=3{p}^{2}q\), where \(p=b+a\) and \(q=b-a\), and express \({p}^{2}\) in terms of \(q\). Deduce that \(1<b-a\le \frac{4}{3}\)
\text{\[\frac{q(3p^2+q^2)}{12}=\frac{p^2q^2}4\]\[3p^2+q^2=3p^2q,\qquad p^2=\frac{q^2}{3(q-1)}\]Positivity gives q > 1. Since a ≥ 0, p ≥ q, so \[\frac1{3(q-1)}\ge1\Rightarrow1<q\le\frac43\]}
